In the school library in Lisbon, Lucia, fifteen, pulled Esther's genetics worksheet across the table. "Okay, it's simple. Brown is dominant, blue is recessive. Both parents are heterozygous, so you cross the alleles in the Punnett square and you get a three-to-one phenotype ratio. Done."
Esther stared at the empty grid. "What's a heterozygous?"
"Big B, small b. Two different alleles." Lucia was already filling in the boxes. "BB, Bb, Bb, bb. See?"
"Why are there four boxes?"
Lucia sighed and put down her pencil. "Esther, we did this for two weeks." She glanced at the clock, then back at the worksheet, tapping it. Honestly, she thought, it's the easiest chapter in the whole book.
Esther closed her notebook. "I'll ask Mr Pinto tomorrow."
Lucia watched her go, puzzled that anyone could find it hard.

qa.q: What ratio did Lucia say you get in the Punnett square?
qa.a: A three-to-one phenotype ratio.

qa.q: Why does Lucia think Esther is being slow?
qa.a: The chapter feels so easy to Lucia that she can't see which steps are missing for a beginner, like what "heterozygous" means or why the grid has four boxes.

qa.q: What could Lucia try next time she explains genetics to a classmate?
qa.a: She could start from the beginning with one plain example, like eye colour in one family, skip the jargon, and ask Esther to explain it back before moving on.

qa.q: What is it like for Esther to be helped this way?
qa.a: It is confusing and a little embarrassing; Esther's simple questions get sighs, so she gives up and decides to ask the teacher instead.

grounding: It shows a teenager who knows genetics well explaining too fast with jargon and thinking her classmate is slow.

"So you just take the PWM pin to the motor driver, set the duty cycle, and ground everything common," Saurabh said, plugging wires in fast. "Then the IR sensor reads high or low and you write an if-else."

I'm Gurleen, and I was in the second row for the NSS orientation when Nilesh, our final-year volunteer lead, gave his talk to about eighty first-years.
He opened with: "So this term we continue the WASH audit in Khanpur, finish the DPR, and hand the O&M plan to the SHG as per the SBM guidelines."
I watched the faces around me. The boy next to me looked at his friend. A girl in front wrote "DPR??" in her notebook. Within a minute, three people were on their phones.
Nilesh kept going, faster, clicking through slides of charts. When someone at the back finally asked, "Sorry, what does WASH mean?", he paused and said, a bit sharply, "It's on the first slide," though it wasn't.
Afterwards he told me, "Nobody here even cares." I'm not sure that was true. They just didn't know what he was talking about.

qa.q: What did the girl in front write in her notebook?
qa.a: She wrote "DPR??" in her notebook.

qa.q: What does Nilesh's sharp reply and his comment afterwards suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: He seemed irritated and resentful, blaming the first-years for not caring, because the acronyms were so familiar to him that he didn't see he had lost them.

qa.q: What went wrong in the first minute, and what could fix it next time?
qa.a: He started with acronyms nobody knew; he could open with one plain story of what the volunteers actually did in Khanpur and explain each short form the first time.

qa.q: How does Gurleen see the first-years' reaction differently from Nilesh?
qa.a: Gurleen thinks they weren't bored or uncaring; they simply didn't understand the words, which is why they drifted to their phones.

grounding: It shows a student presenter assuming first-years know the acronyms and background, and losing them in the first minute.

Gautam, you want to know how to explain your work to people who aren't engineers? Let your Jaya Ammamma tell you about the cyclone of '86.
I was twenty-five, a new forecaster at the weather office in Visakhapatnam, and I had to write the warning for the fishing villages. My first draft said "a deep depression is likely to intensify with a storm surge of two metres". Accurate. Useless.
So I walked to my neighbour Rathnam, who sold fish, and read it to her. She said, "Is depression when you're sad?"
I started again. "A strong storm is coming. The sea will rise higher than your boat is tall. Pull the boats up past the temple steps by tomorrow night." Then I asked her, "Tell me what you'd do." She said it back perfectly.
That went on the radio, word for word, and nobody from those villages went out to sea.

qa.q: Who did Jaya read her first draft to?
qa.a: To her neighbour Rathnam, who sold fish.

qa.q: What did Jaya realise when Rathnam asked if depression meant being sad?
qa.a: She realised her accurate forecasting words meant nothing to the people who needed the warning, so the draft would be useless to them.

qa.q: Which steps made Jaya's warning work?
qa.a: Testing it on someone outside the field, using an example they knew (the sea rising higher than a boat), and asking Rathnam to say back what she would do.

qa.q: How might Rathnam have felt being asked to test the warning?
qa.a: Rathnam may have felt respected and useful, since her plain question shaped a warning that kept her neighbours safe.

grounding: It shows a skilled professional testing her explanation on someone outside the field, using plain words and examples, and asking the listener to say it back.

The residents' meeting in Aizawl started in twenty minutes, the rain was drumming on the tin roof, and Lalremsiami's laptop battery had just died. Her slides on the building's earthquake retrofit were gone.
She was twenty-five, a structural engineer, and she knew every term: shear wall, lateral load, ductile detailing. None of it would work in that room.
Her landlady Shalini was folding clothes in the next room. "Aunty, can I try something on you? Two minutes."
She held up a steel shelf. "If this shelf shakes and it isn't fixed to the wall, it falls. If I bolt it to the wall, it only rattles. We want to do that to the whole building: bolt it to strong walls so it rattles instead of falling."
Shalini nodded slowly. "Say it back to me," Lalremsiami said.
"The building gets tied to strong walls, so it shakes but doesn't fall."
Lalremsiami grinned and grabbed her umbrella.

qa.q: What happened to Lalremsiami's laptop just before the meeting?
qa.a: Its battery had just died, and her slides were gone.

qa.q: What was Lalremsiami thinking about the technical terms she knew?
qa.a: She knew terms like shear wall and lateral load but was sure none of them would work with the residents, so she needed plain words instead.

qa.q: Which choice turned the dead laptop into an advantage?
qa.a: Testing her explanation on Shalini with a shelf as an everyday example and asking her to say it back, which gave Lalremsiami a clear, checked message for the meeting.

qa.q: How might the residents feel hearing the shelf explanation instead of the slides?
qa.a: They would likely feel included and less anxious, because they could picture what the work does to their building without needing engineering words.

grounding: It shows a skilled professional testing her explanation on someone outside the field, using an everyday example and plain words, and asking the listener to say it back.

I'm Chandrika. My sister Amandeep, nineteen, came with us to Nani's house in Shimla for the winter break, and I spent most of it watching the top of her head.
She scrolled at breakfast: a fire somewhere, a scam, an angry thread. She scrolled on the walk to the Mall Road and walked into a lamp post. On the second night it snowed for the first time in years. Nani and I were at the window shouting for her. She came, looked for a second, then went back to a video about some crime.
At dinner she said, "Honestly, the world is getting worse every day. It's all falling apart." Nani asked what had actually changed since last week. Amandeep couldn't name anything; she just said, "Everything."
I don't know what she was feeling. She looked tired, and her jaw was tight all week.

qa.a: She walked into a lamp post.

qa.q: What does Amandeep's comment at dinner suggest about how she sees the world?

qa.q: How could Nani's question help Amandeep, and what small step might follow?
qa.a: Asking what had actually changed shows that her fear has grown without new facts; a small step would be to put the phone away for moments like the first snowfall.

qa.a: Chandrika spent it watching Amandeep's head bent over the phone, missing shared moments like the snow, and seems worried about Amandeep's tight jaw.
